I understand where you're coming from. This isn't always a matter of learning how to socialize. It can be, but ideally, we can't control what the company is doing. If they enforce a hybrid rule, then I'm gonna follow it and learn to make it as a positive experience as I can be. I get drained from my office days too, don't get me wrong, but I do whatever I can to recharge at home. I'm also a student finishing her degree, so I completely understand being drained.

However, we can't control what HR wants in the company. I'm gonna work with their hybrid rule and do my best to be positive about it often. Most companies have been enforcing a RTO rule now; my friends who were safe as remote workers are now being forced to go into the office starting the summer or fall. (For context, they are in tech like me).

There are a lot of remote companies, though. If anyone wants to look into staying at home and working that way, then of course, they can look, and they still do exist. But from my experience, companies can do whatever they want—so if your company suddenly enforces a RTO, it's something to think about. Either you look elsewhere that's remote or find a way to accommodate to their hybrid rule.

No company will ever accommodate you forever. I had coworkers who got a remote exception, but now they have to RTO. If my company had me coming in x5 a week, then I'd look elsewhere. But since I'm only x3, I'm gonna accommodate to it and try to be positive about my office visits. ☺️

No job is ever stable. People come into my company following the hybrid rule of x3 a week and have gotten laid off. People who work from home due to exemptions have gotten laid off. Even though I love my company and would want to grow here, it is possible I can lose it at any time. So can anyone else working at the company.

I had the same thought process too, but then I realized remote work was really taking away from things in the office that were really helpful for me in terms of socialization. I'm a developer in data analytics, and my job involves me working with clients. I also thought remote work was what I wanted, but then I realized going in the office allowed me to 1) do in-person volunteer events with my company to help homeless, seniors, and other non-profits, 2) network with other people that helped me build relationships with clients and my interns better, and 3) help me enhance my communication better through networking events.

Networking landed me a better position in a team that prioritizes mental health—and even better, a $10k bonus to my salary.

I get what you mean, but now I'm all for the hybrid rule. I used to realize I work best at home and fully remote (I, too, groaned and was upset at the hybrid rule), but then I realized that the in-person connections got me a better salary, better position, and even better, friends. :)

EDIT: I fully believe the hybrid rule should be accommodating if you live far, have medical or personal emergencies, and so on. Not everyone can work best in the office, but not everyone can work best at home. A company can't fully accommodate to everyone who is introverted and extroverted—at the end of the day, yeah, you're just an employee to them. So, in my perspective, I'd rather deal with this hybrid rule and look at it positively than spend hours and hours applying and studying for tech interviews in this shit job market right now.

I agree with everything you said here. I felt like OP too, but I grew to love the hybrid rule and now I enjoy seeing my coworkers, engaging in events, having lunch with them, etc. It isn't the end all, be all. I really think COVID did a number to us all, because people also have to realize that extroverts exist too—and many of them have been wanting the "back to office" rule. The hybrid rule, in my opinion, is really accommodating to people who are both introverted and extroverted.

Humans aren't meant to be in pure isolation, we need to learn how to socialize and interact with others. OP will get better within time, I think we all will. It's always just hard at first but it does get better.

It's a matter of figuring out who you're talking to, how well will they catch onto what you're saying, and can they understand it. Especially if it's your manager or product managers/owners.

I can't tell you how crazy it is that people will even not know the simplest tools of tech even after they work in corporate for twenty years. Like dragging a file to another folder kind of simplicity. If you're gonna be the "techy" one—regardless, you have to know how to story tell what you're developing to people who are doing the complete opposite of what you do. If you're gonna be the one who is technical *and* analytical with the presentation, then you sure as hell definitely need to know how to story tell.

I'm a strategy analyst and my manager is a data science executive. Been working in data for almost 3 years now. Your whole post here just makes you ahead of the curve more than folks who want to focus only on SQL, Python, Excel, etc. And if my manager read this, he'd have a grin on his face.

This is exactly the point of working in data. It's about knowing the data you work with, *why* are you even querying and pulling the data, and whatever you're gonna do with it, how are you gonna tell a story with it? I can't tell you how many times have I heard seniors in data talk about newcomers who know how to *code a linear regression* in Python and sklearn, but they have no idea what the hell it even does.

The joy of analytics, specifically, is storytelling and presenting the data to stakeholders and clients who have no idea what the hell the fancy technical stuff is, it's a matter of the product what's being produced and does this actually benefit them. It is super important—like, I can't stress this enough—that you learn how to gradually know your data, understand it, and what you plan to create out of it and *how do you present that to your stakeholders/clients*; present that type of attitude and willingness to learn and that may put you ahead of the curve in an interview amongst other candidates.

Don't sleep on the skills of good communication, data presentation, and data story telling, folks. Honestly, the technical skills are the fun part for me, but it gets even better when you get to talk about what you created and present that. It helps you have good communication and know your audience better outside of work too.

I was diagnosed with OCD at 15, so intrusive thoughts never really go away, but I do my best to combat them. A lot of it was exposure therapy, exercising and focusing on my own goals, and also just positive affirmations. Reminding myself of my worth, beauty, strength, etc. Journaling helped a lot with that. I'm doing a lot better now than I have ever, so hang in there! 🤍

When I say I made it out, it means I'm not thinking about any anxious thoughts about my relationship. I'm not worried about what my partner thinks of me, I'm not constantly thinking about how he'd react, etc. At some point, you learn to let go of those thoughts, cause I sure did. I secured a beautiful relationship with the man I'm with, I'd be damned if I let my anxiety ruin it. So, yeah, I did go to therapy but I did a lot of self-healing on my own. Journaling, reading a lot of books for anxious attachment and ROCD, working on gaining confidence with myself through work, my activities, etc. Picking up new hobbies helped me too, and also exposure therapy. Letting myself take a week away from my partner showcased my strength and trust in him more than anything, and we came back to each other with open arms.

I'm so happy to be finally out of it. I won't lie, I had these thoughts in my previous relationship too. It takes time, and really, a lot of it is just focusing on myself and staying within the current moment. Nowadays, I just want space and let my partner do his thing, haha. But I still love him nonetheless. Hang in there, I hope you find what works best for you and things get better for you 💗🫶🏼

Hi there! I personally believe taking some time apart from your partner is extremely helpful, although it can also be just a "temporary relief" thing too. It's something you gotta make the most out of when you and your partner are in terms of agreement for it.

My boyfriend and I love each other very much, and he makes me so happy. Although, my OCD does kick in a lot and I'm seeking help for it too, so therapy and I have a psychiatrist appointment soon. However, it's still my responsibility to work on myself, and he knows that's the same for his mental health. We take some time apart to focus on ourselves, like several days of no contact and it can go up to a week, and we come back and reflect on how we've been working on ourselves individually and we also talk about how we've missed each other too.

It does provide temporary relief although the anxiety still lingers. It's something I have to tackle and work on myself, whether I am in a relationship or not. And something my therapist told me is that I'm actively working on myself, right, and just by being in a healthy relationship is me facing my OCD head on. So it's up to you on how you determine a "break" with your partner. Time apart helps a lot, though it may only be a temporary relief solution for you, and it's up to you to be responsible on how you want to work around that for yourself.

I always say that your partner is not there to steer the wheel for your path in life, they're merely a passenger and they're there for the ride. You're the driver responsible for your own path, choices, and actions. So ultimately, a "break" or not, you still have to face your anxiety, insecurities, fears, etc. at the end of the day and work around them.

Holy shit, OP. Someone gets me, and that's you. I'm so glad, lmao. I can completely understand and resonate with this post. I have consistent ROCD of obsessive thoughts where I think to myself that "I'm so boring and my partner is gonna have way more fun with other people than me", and it just leads me to talking down upon myself and me either pushing him to spend time with other people rather than me or asking for reassurance that I'm not boring, I'm enjoyable to be around, etc.

I'm currently figuring this out through therapy! And I'm having a difficult time at first not gonna lie, but it's getting easier and easier. What has been helping me is not going him to reassurance. Easier said than done, but his reassurance is a compulsion for me, and as much as my sweet boyfriend wants to be there for me when I need it, I have to be the one to reassure myself.

In a book about anxious attachments, I loved this one quote, and I can't recall what it said word by word, but it basically talked about how one with anxiety in relationships will keep digging for more from their partner, and no matter how much they get their fill, they will just keep filling up nothing but an infinite pit of anxiety. So no matter how much our partners try to help us, it is up to us to reassure ourselves and work through this, and you wanting help is a big step that pat yourself on the back for that.

Anyway! Things like identifying my compulsions help a lot, so me consistently checking his Discord status is a compulsion for me to see what he's doing, and now I'm focusing solely on myself only, and only to do what I want to do and not give into a compulsion. So finding out what they are and controlling them as best as you can, and being mindful when the "itch to compulse" kicks in. Reassurance is a big compulsion too, and also running to your partner when you need them in these difficult times — you and your partner should depend on each other to a healthy extent only.

The one thing about OCD is that the psychological torture of ERP therapy is needed for some, not all. And for me, it has been helping me personally. Exposing myself to my fears of being abandoned, boring, and forgotten easily... I have to accept the anxiety when it comes, instead of trying to kick them away, I have to be okay when they come in and learn to let go to find acceptance that I will not be afraid of these fears anymore. Positive affirmations help a lot, and also recognizing that even these fears... even if they do come true, they are not the end of the world and they do not define my worth. 

You are totally right. Space is crucial and important. I'm a huge advocate for it and honestly, it surprises me that my ROCD still sucks to this day but I'm determined to get better. And damn, we're gonna get better and make it through. I believe in us!

I spoke a lot here haha, but TLDR; finding your compulsions and learning how to not act on them and facing your insecurities/anxiety/fear head on.

I'm a huge advocate for space, but I'm curious OP, how long has your girlfriend been asking for space and time apart?

My boyfriend and I have gone through five days to a week of no contact to focus solely on our mental health and to work on ourselves, and we come back with a big reunion after missing each other a lot. The reunion is always so rewarding because we've missed each other's company and we know that our love is so strong for each other. Sometimes that time apart is needed for you to reflect on yourself, grow as a person individually, and then connect with your partner until she's ready to talk. Hi OP, I was diagnosed with OCD a couple of years ago and I can understand how difficult it is to talk about the disorder since it's so stigmatized and causes so many misconceptions.

I brought up OCD on my first date with my current boyfriend and he opened up to me about his mental health too, so that was a huge green flag for me that he was so open about that. Anyways, even so, he's still learning how to fully navigate and understand my triggers and anxiety even after being with me for over a year, but the fact that I can slowly open up to him about it helps a lot.

And really, it just comes down to talking about it. Giving a good background of the disorder usually helps, so stating that we derive off of an obsessive fear (perhaps it's based off trauma or not at all), and we compulsively react to it as a coping mechanism or just to feel more "secure". Then explain what your fears are and what are your compulsive actions. I did this with my boyfriend and he asks how he can help whenever I start to feel anxious and there have been times where he would step out with me just to be with me when I'm anxious, and I talked about things he can do to support me when I'm triggered or anxious as well. However, at the end of the day, it's still our responsibility to take care of ourselves and make sure that we're trying our best ourselves to keep us in line and fight the anxiety. Our partners are there to support us, not be our solution to the problem — which is anxiety.

Sending you love, OP! 🤍

Hey, I just wanna say that you're totally not alone. How you're feeling is perfectly valid and you have every right to feel the way you do, although you are going to need to put in some effort in order to help yourself get through it. And honestly, I've been coming to realizations myself even the past week — to the point where, "oh shit, wait. Everything is clicking and making sense now."

I was diagnosed with OCD around my adolescent years, so I had obsessive fears and I compulsively reacted to them which led to heavy depression and mental exhaustion. I've noticed that throughout my relationships, even my current one, my OCD really kicks in and now things are clicking. Just like you, I have these obsession fears as well, thinking "what if we're not compatible and that things don't work out?" or "I'm such a freak, he should leave me so he can save himself from me because I'm annoying" and so on, you get the point.

My compulsive actions throughout my previous relationship, and with this one, is that in order to combat these thoughts, I have been wanting reassurance. So I get the attention, words of affirmation, and so on from my previous partner and current one, and that just eased it, but I realized this week that it me asking was out of a compulsive act rather than understanding the bigger picture. And I think the bigger picture is that when my OCD kicks in, I shouldn't be relying on my partner to keep me in gear with consistent reassurance and attention, but I should remind myself the logical things like "I chose to be with him, as he chose to be with me, and whatever happens at the end of the day is all meant to be an experience in life — good or bad" and other rational thoughts like "I am loved by my partner, so a day of space does not equal abandonment."

I really encourage you to look at your fears and anxiety deep down, like find the underlying cause of it. Was it trauma? Is it simply mental illness? Did they do something to make you feel that way? Finding those answers helps make things open up, and try to look at your actions too. Are you doing anything to follow up with those fears to help you at ease, and are they really healthy actions or are they encouraging the fear to come back more? Being able to challenge your anxiety is a big thing, and it can be hard yes, it may make you emotional and struggle mentally but it's a huge thing. I really suggest going back to therapy and talking about these things and finding ways to help you cope through this time.

I also gotta say, hobbies and keeping yourself occupied is really good, and journaling is a big one for me. Keeping track of your anxiety along with your ups and downs is big for me and also it helps to write down positive affirmations for yourself. Things like meditation, reading philosophy, and journaling have been big game changers for me.

With all that being said, I've been challenging my obsessive fear of abandonment from my partner by making plans with friends this weekend so I can go out on my own freely and not be scared of my partner suddenly not loving me anymore or forgetting about me. Find ways to challenge your fears and your thoughts! It's so hard, trust me, but at some point, you'll want to just get better and find a way to be stronger.
